rics.meaning: M0 / Monetary Base — currency in circulation + bank reserves at Fed. The Fed's direct liquidity injection.
rics.how_to_use: QE expanded the base 5x post-2008. Now shrinking via QT. Loose proxy for Fed balance sheet liquidity. Reserves portion specifically determines money market dynamics (RRP, fed funds market activity).

rics.description: Money Supply M0, Standardized, Chg P/P
rics.meaning: Money supply M0 MoM % change.
rics.how_to_use: Volatile during balance-sheet operations. Less informative than YoY.

rics.description: Money Supply M0, Standardized, Chg Y/Y
rics.meaning: Money supply M0 YoY % change.
rics.how_to_use: Useful long-run liquidity-cycle gauge. Negative growth = active QT.

rics.meaning: M1 Money Supply — currency + checking deposits + traveler's checks. Pre-2020 definition.
rics.how_to_use: Definition expanded in May 2020 to INCLUDE savings deposits — the level jumped artificially. Pre-2020 M1 series not directly comparable to post-2020. Use M2 for cleaner historical analysis.

rics.description: Money Supply M1, Standardized, Chg P/P
rics.meaning: Money Supply M1 standardized, MoM percent change — monthly growth rate of M1 (currency + demand deposits + savings deposits post-2020 reclassification).
rics.how_to_use: Highly volatile post-2020 due to M1 reclassification. Watch year-over-year (aUSCMS1YB/A) for trend. Sustained negative monthly readings rare but happened in 2022-23 during QT.

rics.description: Money Supply M1, Standardized, Chg Y/Y
rics.meaning: M1 YoY % change.
rics.how_to_use: Cross-check M1 vs M2 growth — divergence reveals whether liquidity is in transactional vs savings accounts.

rics.description: Money Supply M2, % month on month, Standardized, Chg P/P
rics.meaning: Money Supply M2, MoM percent change — monthly growth rate of broad M2 aggregate. The most-watched money-supply growth signal.
rics.how_to_use: Watch for sustained MoM contractions as monetary-tightening signals. 2022-23 saw rare M2 contractions during QT — contributed to disinflation. Compare to nominal GDP for velocity-implied trend.

rics.description: Money Supply M2, % year on year, Standardized, Chg Y/Y
rics.meaning: M2 YoY % change — the most-watched money supply growth rate.
rics.how_to_use: Loose proxy for inflation 12-18 months out (monetarist view; weak in practice). Surged to 27% in 2021 post-stimulus, contracted in 2023. Sustained negative M2 growth historically associated with recession.

rics.meaning: M2 Money Supply level, standardized — M1 + small time deposits + retail money funds. The broadest practical money supply measure.
rics.how_to_use: M3 was discontinued in 2006. M2 surged 27% YoY in 2021 post-stimulus, contracted in 2023 (first sustained negative since 1930s). Watch nominal growth rate vs nominal GDP growth.

rics.meaning: Adjusted reserves — bank reserves at the Fed, adjusted for changes in reserve requirements.
rics.how_to_use: Matters for the federal funds market. Reserves abundance reduces fed funds market activity (since 2008).

rics.meaning: Adjusted monetary base — Fed's preferred monetary-base measure adjusted for changes in reserve requirements and required-reserve ratio shifts. Most consistent across regulatory regimes.
rics.how_to_use: Cleaner than the raw monetary base for long-time-series comparisons. Post-2008 the distinction matters less because reserve requirements were eliminated in 2020. Track for Fed balance-sheet trajectory.

rics.meaning: M2 velocity — nominal GDP divided by M2 money stock. Measures how often each dollar circulates per year in nominal output.
rics.how_to_use: Post-2008 collapsed from ~2.0 to ~1.1 as M2 expanded faster than nominal GDP. A revival of velocity is a pre-condition for sustained inflation: more money + same velocity = inflation; more money + falling velocity = deflation pressure.

rics.description: H.6, U.S. government deposits, total cash balance
rics.meaning: H.6 — US government deposits, Treasury General Account (TGA) at Fed.
rics.how_to_use: TGA is a major liquidity siphon. When Treasury rebuilds TGA after a debt-ceiling deal, bank reserves drain — funding stress risk.

rics.meaning: Monetary base (Fed H.3 release) — currency in circulation plus bank reserves at the Fed. Direct Fed liability; expands with QE, contracts with QT. Distinct from broader money aggregates.
rics.how_to_use: Misleading as a 'money supply' indicator post-2008 because reserves became huge but velocity collapsed (banks held them rather than lend). Useful for tracking Fed balance-sheet operations directly. Compare to M2 for the bank-lending multiplier.

rics.meaning: MZM (Money of Zero Maturity) money stock — all money instantly convertible to cash without penalty. Effectively M2 minus small time deposits plus all institutional money funds.
rics.how_to_use: Less commonly tracked since the Fed discontinued its publication; private compilations remain. Some monetarists consider MZM more economically meaningful than M2 because time deposits are illiquid for transactional purposes.

rics.meaning: M1 money supply (annual aggregate) — companion to monthly aUSM1 at lower frequency. Same conceptual measure.
rics.how_to_use: Use monthly aUSM1 for high-frequency tracking. Annual aggregate useful for long-time-series analysis. Post-2020 M1 includes savings deposits — the M1 vs M2 distinction is now blurred.

rics.meaning: M1 money supply — currency in circulation + demand deposits + savings deposits (post-May 2020 reclassification, which made M1 ≈ M2 minus small time deposits and money-market mutual funds).
rics.how_to_use: Post-2020 the M1 vs M2 distinction blurred — savings deposits were moved from M2 into M1. Watch M2 instead for the meaningful aggregate. M1 still useful for tracking high-liquidity household balances; spikes during stress (cash hoarding) and post-stimulus.

rics.meaning: M1 money supply, weekly — Fed H.6 release at weekly frequency. Smoother than monthly because it's a weekly average.
rics.how_to_use: Track for high-frequency M1 movements. Useful for spotting sudden shifts in liquidity preference (cash hoarding, deposit flight). Pair with weekly M2 (aUSM2W) for full picture.

rics.meaning: M1 money supply, weekly (alternate release) — same conceptual measure as aUSM1W/A.
rics.how_to_use: Cross-check series. Use whichever is fresher.

rics.meaning: M2 money supply (annual aggregate) — companion to monthly aUSM2 at lower frequency.
rics.how_to_use: Use monthly aUSM2 for high-frequency tracking. Annual aggregate useful for long-time-series analysis.

rics.meaning: M2 money supply — M1 + small time deposits + retail money-market mutual funds. The broadest commonly-tracked monetary aggregate; includes most household liquid savings.
rics.how_to_use: Year-over-year M2 growth is the key indicator. Sustained M2 contraction is rare — happened in 2022-23 for the first time in modern data, contributing to disinflation pressure. Fast M2 growth (>10% YoY like 2020) tends to precede inflation surges with 12-18mo lag.

rics.meaning: M2 money supply, weekly — Fed H.6 release at weekly frequency. Most-watched high-frequency money-supply gauge.
rics.how_to_use: Tracks broad money at weekly resolution. Useful for spotting policy-effect timing: M2 acceleration signals expansion phase; sustained contraction signals tightening pressure (rare, observed 2022-23).

rics.meaning: M2 money supply, weekly (alternate release) — same conceptual measure as aUSM2W/A.
rics.how_to_use: Cross-check series. Use whichever has fresher data.
